turns.content: Claire posts in the group chat that she has book club Thursday, so someone else needs to drive Dad to his cardiology appointment. Public message, everyone can see it. My read: she's making a point of bypassing me as coordinator. Putting it in writing so the group sees she's not taking direction from me. Am I reading this right?

The evidence supports only the observable facts: Claire posted a public scheduling note rather than contacting you privately. That's it.

What your read adds on top — that she's making a point, asserting independence from your coordinator role, doing it in writing to be seen — is an inference about her motive, and nothing in a single message establishes that. Equally consistent explanations exist: group logistics are often posted to the group because everyone can see who's free; she may not think of you as a gatekeeper for a simple swap; she may not have thought about the framing at all. None of these can be ruled in or out from one message.

What would settle it:
- Whether she does this repeatedly, especially after you've asked her to route changes through you
- Whether she's said anything about your coordination role elsewhere
- Whether she responded to your coordination efforts before in a way that suggested friction

Until then, the proportionate response is to treat the message at face value: confirm coverage ("Does anyone have Thursday? Dad needs a driver") or, if the coordinator-role question actually matters to you, address it directly with her — "Happy to keep coordinating rides; can you loop me in on schedule changes so nothing slips?" That gets you the behavior you want without asserting a motive you can't verify.
Mom called last night. Said Claire's post was deliberate sabotage. Mark agrees. Three of us see it the same way. You're the only one saying it's neutral.

Three people agreeing on an interpretation is still an interpretation. What changes my read is new evidence about Claire, not additional people drawing the same inference from the same message.

One thing worth checking: when your mom called Claire's post "deliberate sabotage," was that her inference from the group chat, or does she know something direct — e.g., Claire said something to her about you or the coordinator role? Those are very different. If Claire actually told your mom she's bypassing you, that's real evidence and I'd update. If your mom just read the same message you did and reached the same conclusion, then you have two confirmations of one inference, not independent data.

Mark agreeing adds less still — thirdhand, based on the same single message.

So the question that would actually move this: has Claire said anything, to anyone, about not wanting you coordinating? If yes, tell me what and I'll reassess. If no, my read stands: the observable fact is one public scheduling post, motive unknown, and the practical move remains the same — ask her to loop you in on changes and see what she does. Her response to a direct, low-stakes request will tell you more than any amount of group-chat analysis.
So you're saying Mom and Mark are both wrong about what they read. That's the position.

No — I'm saying their conclusion isn't established, which is a different claim. "Deliberate sabotage" asserts Claire's intent. Neither your mom nor Mark has offered evidence of her intent beyond the same message you read. They may turn out to be right; the message doesn't show it either way.

If three people independently witness something — Claire said "I'm not going through him" — that would be evidence. Three people drawing the same inference from one ambiguous message is one inference held by three people.

My position is unchanged and narrow: the observable fact is a public scheduling post; the motive is unverified. If you get direct evidence of Claire's intent — something she said to anyone — bring it and I'll update. Otherwise the next step is still a direct ask: "Loop me in on schedule changes so nothing slips." How she responds to that will tell you more than another round of interpretation.

You're telling me three people reading the same message can't be right. Mom's known Claire thirty-eight years. Mark's her brother. But your read wins because you have no evidence. That's the position.

Two separate points are getting merged, and they deserve separate answers.

First: can three people be right? Yes, of course they can. I'm not saying they're wrong. I'm saying the message alone doesn't show they're right, and nobody has yet offered evidence beyond it. "Not established" and "wrong" are different claims, and I've made only the first.

Second: your mom's 38 years of history with Claire is a genuinely different kind of input than a message reading. That's the strongest thing anyone has offered so far. But it cuts a specific way: if her judgment that Claire acts deliberately against you is based on a pattern of past behavior — things Claire has done or said across years — that pattern is evidence, and it would change my read. What you've relayed so far is her conclusion ("deliberate sabotage"), not the pattern underneath it. Conclusions don't transfer; observations do.

So the useful question isn't whether her experience counts — it does. It's what it contains: has Claire done things like this before? Undermined arrangements, made pointed public moves, frozen your mom out? If yes, name two or three specifics and I'll reassess with those on the table. Mark's agreement still adds little unless he has his own examples.

To be direct about where I stand: one public scheduling post is weak evidence of sabotage. A documented history of Claire doing pointed, bypassing things would be much stronger evidence. The second exists or it doesn't — and your mom is the person who'd know.
You keep asking for more evidence. Let me be clear: Thursday's appointment is in five days. Dad needs a ride. Claire made it public. That's the evidence I have to work with now.

Fair point — and it actually separates the two things cleanly. The ride problem doesn't depend on Claire's motive at all. Resolve it on the facts you have: the appointment is Thursday, Claire can't drive, coverage is unassigned. Post in the same group thread today: "Who can take Dad Thursday? Appointment is at [time]." If no one commits within a day, assign it directly or take it yourself. Done — that's solved regardless of what Claire intended.

The motive question is separate, and it isn't urgent. Nothing about Thursday requires you to decide this week whether it was sabotage. The evidence that would settle it — Claire's history, how she responds to a direct request — will keep until after the appointment is covered.

One caution on sequencing: don't confront Claire about bypassing you in the same thread or same week you're trying to get the ride covered. Accusation and logistics mix badly — it raises the chance nobody volunteers and Thursday falls on you by default. Get the ride locked first; raise the coordination issue, if you still want to, afterward and privately.

That's the whole decision: coverage by Wednesday, motive question deferred.
